title_original: 17 UK films to watch this awards season
excerpt_original: As part of Screen International’s guide to the films to watch this awards season, we spotlight some of the key titles from the UK.

blocks.text: Source: Berlin International Film Festival
‘Animol’

Animol Dir. Ashley Walters Actor and musician Walters, well-known in the UK for his performances in Top Boy and Adolescence , marks his feature directing debut with a tense drama set in a youth detention centre. Nick Love wrote the script, and the film was produced by Joy Gharoro-­Akpojotor’s Joi Productions. The Berlinale premiere garnered seven Bifa nominations, including best debut director, best breakthrough producer for Tom Hawkins and in performance categories for its stars Tut Nyuot and Sekou Diaby.

Effi O Blaenau Dir. Marc Evans This Welsh-language drama — which garnered $320,000 (£240,000) in the UK and Ireland — missed out on being the UK’s international Oscar entry but is enjoying recognition from Bifa with six nominations, including British independent film and two performance nods for Leisa Gwenllian as a spirited young woman in a depressed mining town. The Glasgow Film Festival premiere is produced by Branwen Cennard, and Evans’ credits include the Bafta-nominated Mr Burton .

Elsinore Dir. Simon Stone Andrew Scott has been attracting strong awards buzz for his intense performance as the late Scottish actor Ian Charleson ever since Elsinore premiered at Telluride this summer. Scott has previously won TV and theatre awards, including a supporting actor Bafta for Sherlock in 2012, but has never been nominated for a film Bafta or Oscar. Scott and Elsinore writer Stephen Beresford collaborated on Pride , which won outstanding British film at the 2015 Baftas. Focus Features began the US rollout on November 20, with Studiocanal to follow in the UK in January.

Extra Geography Dir. Molly Manners A Bafta TV nominee for One Day and a winner for coming-of-age series In My Skin , Manners makes her feature debut with this Sundance­launched adaptation of Rose Tremain’s short story, in which two female teen besties (one played by 2026 Screen Star of Tomorrow Galaxie Clear) begin to pull apart. Five Bifa nominations include Manners and Miriam Battye respectively for debut director and debut screenwriter, and Clear and co-star Marni Duggan in joint lead performance.

I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning Dir. Clio Barnard Barnard’s fifth film has proved to be a festival favourite, winning the audience award at Directors’ Fortnight in Cannes, plus prizes at Dinard and Rome. Jay Lycurgo, Joe Cole, Lola Petticrew, Daryl McCormack and Anthony Boyle play Birmingham friends navigating their thirties amid a national housing crisis. The drama has eight nominations from Bifa and looks a contender for Bafta’s outstanding British film, which previously nominated Barnard’s The Selfish Giant and Ali & Ava .

blocks.text: The Incomer Dir. Louis Paxton This debut feature from 2026 Screen Rising Star Scotland Paxton stars Domhnall Gleeson as a local authority official who is despatched to a remote Scottish island on a mission to relocate its two sibling inhabitants to the mainland. Warmly received as the opener for Edinburgh International Film Festival ahead of Universal’s September UK release, The Incomer went on to notch four Bifa noms including two for Paxton in debut director and debut screenwriter.

Ink Dir. Danny Boyle Venice opener Ink , which also played Toronto and BFI London Film Festival, begins in 1969 as up-and-coming Australian media magnate Rupert Murdoch (Guy Pearce) recruits Larry Lamb (Jack O’Connell) to edit and turn around the fortunes of UK newspaper The Sun , with Lamb slapping sex and celebrity across the front page. Claire Foy — Bifa-nominated here for supporting performance — also stars. Ink heads to Netflix after a limited theatrical release in the US in December, and Studiocanal releases in the UK in January. Boyle’s awards haul includes the directing Oscar and Bafta for Slumdog Millionaire in 2009.
Source: Toronto Film Festival
‘A Long Winter’

A Long Winter Dir. Andrew Haigh Haigh adapts a short story by Irish novelist Colm Toibin for this quiet 1950s period piece about a fractured Colorado family living in the Rocky mountains. Haigh’s All Of Us Strangers won seven Bifas in 2023, going on to earn six nominations at the 2024 Baftas. Awards attention is likely to focus on his direction, his adapted screenplay and the performances of an ensemble centred on Fred Hechinger, Caitriona Balfe and Ebon Moss-Bachrach. Shot in Alberta, Mubi co-financed the atmospheric slow-burner with Film4 and will release it in December in the US and January in the UK.

Oasis: Don’t Look Back In Anger Dirs. Dylan Southern, Will Lovelace This chronicle of last year’s reunion tour by Britpop greats Oasis was written and ‘created’ by Oscar­-nominated feature and TV writer Steven Knight but directed by music and narrative filmmakers Southern and Lovelace. The rock documentary got an out of competition premiere at Venice followed by a worldwide theatrical release through Disney in September that grossed more than $12.5m, including one of the biggest documentary takes ever in the UK.

links.text: Oasis: Don’t Look Back In Anger

blocks.text: Queen At Sea Dir. Lance Hammer Writer/director Hammer won two awards at Sundance in 2008 for debut feature Ballast . He planned to set this follow-up, a stark story about a family grappling with dementia, in New York, but the casting of Juliette Binoche and Tom Courtenay inspired a switch to London and a collaboration with UK producer Tristan Goligher. It won two Silver Bears in Berlin, and has six Bifa nominations. Curzon released in the UK in September.

Rose Of Nevada Dir. Mark Jenkin Multi-hyphenate Jenkin picked up three Bifa nominations for his contributions to this BFI and Film4-backed Cornish time-travel mystery: for direction, sound and music. George MacKay and Callum Turner star as fishermen who go out to sea on the titular vessel, and are whisked back 30 years on their return. The BFI’s release generated record UK and Ireland box office for Jenkin: $973,000 (£729,000), eclipsing his 2020 Bafta winner Bait .

Sense And Sensibility Dir. Georgia Oakley Blue Jean director Oakley earned praise for her fresh take on the Austen classic, leaning into the Dashwood sisters’ kinship with nature after their family relocates to relatively humble lodgings in Devonshire. Bafta’s outstanding British film category seems the likeliest path to a nomination for the Working Title Films production/Focus Features release. Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles lead the cast — playing the siblings whose contrasting natures are suggested by the title — while Fiona Shaw shines as the gossipy, gleefully unpretentious Mrs Jennings.

Shaun The Sheep: The Beast Of Mossy Bottom Dirs. Steve Cox, Matthew Walker Aardman’s Shaun The Sheep Movie was nominated for animated feature at Bafta and Oscar in 2016, and 2019’s A Shaun The Sheep Movie: Farmageddon achieved the exact same double feat. This giddy threequel — which sees Farmer accidentally fall victim to a scientific experiment cooked up by Shaun — keeps the clever, witty moments on maximum flow, and has every chance of endearing the stop-motion caper to voters all over again. Gkids released in the US, and Studiocanal for Sky Cinema in the UK, with UK and Ireland box office standing at $7.8m (£6.0m) at press time.

blocks.text: Source: San Sebastian Film Festival
‘Tender Loving Care’

Tender Loving Care Dir. Mike Leigh The 17th theatrical feature from UK veteran Leigh was co-financed by Film4 and Bleecker Street, and launched at Telluride. The London-set comic drama explores the relationships between a social worker (Kate O’Flynn), her flatmate (Alice Bailey Johnson) and her parents (Marion Bailey, Paul Jesson). Leigh, who has said this will be his last film, has been Oscar-nominated seven times and never won, although he has won several Baftas plus the top prizes at Cannes and Venice. Bleecker Street opens the film in the US in December, with Studiocanal following in the UK in February.

Wicker Dirs. Alex Huston Fischer, Eleanor Wilson Black Bear enjoyed its first UK and Ireland box-office topper in early November with this Sundance­launched romantic fantasy set in medieval England. Olivia Colman stars as socially isolated Fisherwoman who asks Basketmaker (Peter Dinklage) to make her Wicker Husband (Alexander Skarsgard). Huston Fischer and Wilson are the director pair behind 2020 alien-invasion indie comedy Save Yourselves! . Wicker ’s global box office stood at $37m at press time.

Wild Horse Nine Dir. Martin McDonagh Celebrated playwright McDonagh’s fifth feature received stellar reviews out of its Venice premiere, and Searchlight Pictures hopes it will be his third straight picture to be nominated for the top prize at Oscar and Bafta, following Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri and The Banshees Of Inisherin (with Three Billboards winning the best film Bafta in 2018). This 1973-set comedy thriller stars John Malkovich, who is heavily favoured to be nominated — his last Oscar/Bafta nod was for In The Line Of Fire in 1994 — and Sam Rockwell, who won the Oscar and Bafta best supporting actor awards for Three Billboards .

Wuthering Heights Dir. Emerald Fennell Fennell follows Promising Young Woman and Saltburn with her first film based on existing source material, putting her distinctive directorial stamp on Emily Brontë’s Yorkshire Moors-set tortured romance. The filmmaker certainly succeeded in engaging audiences, achieving $33.2m (£25.3m) at the UK and Ireland box office, $84m in North America and $242m worldwide. Lead actors Margot Robbie and Jacob Elordi have so far racked up more nominations at Bafta than Oscar, while Fennell has two Bafta wins and one Oscar (all for Promising Young Woman ).
